 Follow Dog Owner Shares the Hilarious Reality of Daylight Saving Time With Pets
 Kelly Peacock Tue, November 10, 2026 at 4:55 PM UTC 3 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Dog Owner Shares the Hilarious Reality of Daylight Saving Time With Pets Parade Pets and Yahoo may earn commission from links in this article.
 Twice a year, a familiar event rolls around: daylight saving time. In spring, clocks move forward one hour; in fall, they turn back an hour.
 Most of us are used to this seasonal adjustment, but we may not think about how it affects our pups, who have no concept of clocks or why their dinner suddenly seems late.

 This adorable video from @benny_and_remy on YouTube captures the struggle of dogs trying to understand the time change and, more importantly, how it affects their dinner schedule.
 Dogs Don't Understand the Time Change
 The video features two golden retrievers sticking their noses into their empty food bowls and sniffing around in anticipation. Benny and Remy look up at the camera and their owners with the saddest eyes, wondering why dinner hasn't arrived yet.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Sarah McLachlan's "Angel" plays in the background as on-screen text reads: "Every year, innocent Goldens are forced to wait an extra hour for dinner because of Daylight Saving Time."
 Naturally, viewers couldn't help but sympathize with the hungry pups. One commenter joked, "Terrible situation. Look at their sad faces…it's painful," while another shared their sympathy, writing, "The hardship these poor creatures have to endure."
 Other commenters had a simple solution: Why not move mealtime up so Benny and Remy don't have to suffer?

 How to Help Your Dog Adjust to Daylight Saving Time
 Dogs are creatures of habit. They're used to having meals, walks, playtime, and bedtime at relatively consistent times each day. When the clocks change, that familiar routine can suddenly feel a little different. Your dog might start waking up earlier, asking for breakfast or dinner before their usual mealtime, or showing signs of restlessness as they adjust to the new schedule.
 Advertisement Advertisement One of the best approaches is to gradually adjust your dog's routine rather than changing everything at once.
 Try shifting mealtimes by 10 to 15 minutes over several days leading up to the time change. You can do the same with walks, playtime, and bedtime to help your pup ease into the new schedule. Incorporate indoor enrichment activities, like puzzle toys or training sessions, to keep your dog mentally stimulated.
 Most dogs adjust to the time change without much trouble, but remember that every pup is different. For puppies, senior dogs, or pups who are particularly sensitive to routine changes, a little extra patience and reassurance can go a long way.
 Keep their routine as consistent as possible, offer plenty of affection, and try to be understanding if they're a little confused about why their meals aren't arriving when they expect them.
